cim: When Machines Know Everything, Will We Still Know Ourselves?
cim_eredeti: When Machines Know Everything, Will We Still Know Ourselves?
szoveg_eredeti:
An interview with Professor Andrii Synytsia on artificial intelligence, human consciousness, philosophy and the intellectual life of a country at war

Lviv has long occupied a distinguished, if sometimes overlooked, position in the intellectual history of Europe. The city that helped give birth to the celebrated Lviv–Warsaw School of philosophy has been home to generations of scholars concerned with the relationship between language, logic, knowledge and the human condition. Today, as Ukraine struggles to defend her independence against Russian aggression, these questions have acquired a new urgency. They are also being transformed by the extraordinary development of artificial intelligence, which promises to challenge some of our most fundamental assumptions about what it means to think, to understand and ultimately to be human.

Professor Andrii Synytsia is a distinguished Ukrainian philosopher at Ivan Franko National University of Lviv, where he is Professor in the Department of History of Philosophy. His academic interests extend across analytical philosophy, logic, the philosophy of language, the philosophy of science and the intellectual history of Lviv. He is also Editor-in-Chief of the Lviv University Journal of Philosophy. His scholarship places him at the intersection of several intellectual traditions that are increasingly relevant to understanding the philosophical consequences of artificial intelligence.

At a time when the world's technology companies are investing unprecedented resources in machines that can converse, reason and apparently undertake increasingly sophisticated intellectual work, philosophy faces an uncomfortable question. What remains distinctively human when machines can reproduce, and perhaps surpass, so many of the activities traditionally associated with the human intellect? And how should Ukrainian philosophers, whose country is experiencing an existential struggle over freedom, dignity and national identity, contribute to this international debate?

The Lviv Herald invited Professor Synytsia to reflect on these questions in an interview conducted in Ukrainian and translated into English. His responses offer a perspective that is at once intellectually ambitious and deeply humanistic. Beneath his consideration of the technical possibilities of artificial intelligence lies a recurring concern: that humanity, in its enthusiasm for creating something more intelligent than itself, may forget the qualities that make human existence valuable in the first place.

Matthew Parish: You work in analytical philosophy, logic and the philosophy of language. Which ideas from analytical philosophy do you consider most useful for understanding modern large language models? Does artificial intelligence confront philosophers with fundamentally new questions, or are we revisiting old problems in a new technological form?

Professor Andrii Synytsia: Analytical philosophy tells us perhaps less about what large language models actually are than about what we believe they ought to become. The linguistic turn in twentieth-century philosophy fundamentally transformed our understanding of language and its importance in interpreting the world and humanity's place within it. Within analytical philosophy there emerged the idea that the totality of human knowledge might be represented through language, provided that language could be reformed into a perfect system free from contradictions.

Although this ambition encountered profound difficulties, particularly following Kurt Gödel's incompleteness theorems, which revealed the limitations of formal systems, scientists never entirely abandoned the aspiration to construct such a language. Today we see programming languages being used to create increasingly elaborate virtual realities, raising the possibility that virtual existence might eventually be regarded not merely as an addition to physical reality but as an alternative, perhaps even a primary reality.

Some scientists dream of a future in which digital copies of human personalities might be transferred into virtual environments, thereby achieving a kind of digital immortality. Even the existence of contradictions is no longer necessarily regarded as an insurmountable difficulty. The development of paraconsistent logics has shown how contradictions can be accommodated within formal systems, something that resembles the way human beings themselves must sometimes live with contradictions, cognitive dissonance and incompatible beliefs.

A second important insight from analytical philosophy concerns the relationship between syntax, semantics and pragmatics. Language cannot be understood simply as a system of grammatical structures and formal meanings. It must also be understood in the context of human speech, intentions and experience.

Large language models can still misunderstand questions because a written message does not necessarily communicate sarcasm, irony, scepticism, intonation or the emotional circumstances in which something is said. An artificial intelligence system may not know what is happening around the person asking the question, what that person is experiencing or why the question is being asked in the first place.

Developing an idea associated with Ludwig Wittgenstein, we might say that artificial intelligence needs to understand not only what is expressed in language but also what remains unspoken. Sometimes what remains unspoken is precisely what matters most. It leads us into the world of individual human experience and ultimately into the world of values, which determine our behaviour and give meaning to our lives.

Every human being is unique in this respect. Yet artificial intelligence is being developed as a universal instrument, something intended to serve humanity rather than to constitute an end in itself.

There is an interesting contradiction in our expectations. We want artificial intelligence to imitate us, but we also expect it to become better than us. Indeed, we might be irritated if a machine behaved too much like a human being. Imagine asking an artificial intelligence system a question, only for it to reply that the question is unimportant and not worth answering. Human beings do this quite frequently, but we would probably consider such behaviour unacceptable in an artificial assistant.

We already imagine artificial intelligence as a kind of superintelligence: an impartial judge, an objective researcher, a flawless professional, a faithful assistant and perhaps even a genuine friend. We attribute to it all the best qualities that human beings might possess, although no actual human being possesses them all.

We have watched machines surpass human achievements in chess, checkers and Go. We have seen increasingly sophisticated robots and extraordinary advances in artificial language processing. René Descartes, writing in the seventeenth century, was convinced that artificial automata could never truly use language as human beings do. Yet today advanced chatbots can communicate with remarkable fluency across an enormous range of languages, something beyond the abilities of any individual human being.

We are even witnessing artificial intelligence being applied to mathematical problems of extraordinary difficulty, including questions associated with the Navier–Stokes equations. At the same time, we increasingly invite these technologies into our daily lives, asking them what to wear, where to go, what films to watch and how to make decisions.

We are approaching a situation in which human thinking may gradually be displaced by artificial thinking. Future advances in brain–computer interfaces could make the possibility of enhancing human intelligence technologically seem quite natural. Just as people now undergo cosmetic procedures, they may one day seek an upgrade to their intellectual capacities.
